claim: Mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) cause recurring bacterial infection in CF patients' lungs.
source: Mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) cause recurring bacterial infection in CF patients' lungs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information about CF disease.

claim: The severity of CF lung disease correlates poorly with genotype.
source: However, the severity of CF lung disease correlates poorly with genotype.
evidence: This is stated as a known observation in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Antibiotic treatment helps dramatically prolong CF patients' life.
source: Antibiotic treatment helps dramatically prolong patients' life.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: The lung disease generally determines prognosis and causes most morbidity and mortality in CF patients.
source: The lung disease generally determines prognosis and causes most morbidity and mortality
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about CF disease.

claim: Early control of infections is critical in CF patients.
source: early control of infections is thus critical
evidence: This is stated as a logical conclusion from the severity of lung disease in CF patients.

claim: Staphylococcus aureus is a main cause of early infection in CF lungs.
source: Staphylococcus aureus is a main cause of early infection in CF lungs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation in the introduction.

claim: Staphylococcus aureus secretes sphingomyelinase (SMase) C.
source: It secretes sphingomyelinase (SMase) C
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: SMase C cleaves sphingomyelin into phosphocholine and ceramide.
source: Most S. aureus strains, including methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), secrete the pathogenic factor sphingomyelinase (SMase) C, which cleaves sphingomyelin into phosphocholine and ceramide (Doery et al., 1963) (upper panel, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SMase C can suppress CFTR activity.
source: It secretes sphingomyelinase (SMase) C that can suppress CFTR activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous work cited in the introduction.

claim: SMase C inhibits voltage-gated K+ channels in lymphocytes.
source: SMase C also inhibits voltage-gated K+ channels in lymphocytes
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation in the introduction.

claim: Inhibition of voltage-gated K+ channels causes immunosuppression.
source: inhibition of these channels causes immunosuppression
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation in the introduction.

claim: Bacillus anthracis engineered to express high levels of SMase C can evade host immunity elicited by a live vaccine.
source: once Bacillus anthracis is engineered to express high levels of SMase C, the resulting mutant can evade the host immunity elicited by a live vaccine because additional pathogenic mechanisms are created
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation in the introduction.

claim: Tannic acid is an SMase C antidote.
source: By screening a chemical library, we find that the natural product tannic acid is an SMase C antidote.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data.

claim: CFTR is activated when its regulatory (R) domain is phosphorylated by cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA).
source: The cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) Cl− channel is activated when its regulatory (R) domain is phosphorylated by cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA) (Tabcharani et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Mutations of CFTR cause CF disease that involves multiple organs.
source: Mutations of CFTR cause CF disease that involves multiple organs (Knowles et al., 1983; Kerem et al., 1989; Riordan et al., 1989; Rommens et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: Defective CFTR in CF patients' lungs leads to production of thick mucus that obstructs airways.
source: In the lungs of CF patients, defective CFTR leads to production of thick mucus that obstructs airways
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about CF pathology.

claim: Thick mucus in CF patients' lungs predisposes patients to recurring bacterial infection.
source: defective CFTR leads to production of thick mucus that obstructs airways and thus predisposes the patients to recurring bacterial infection
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about CF pathology.

claim: Aggressive antibiotic treatment and supportive measures have prolonged the median life span of CF patients from 5 to 37 years.
source: Aggressive antibiotic treatment and supportive measures have prolonged the median life span of patients from 5 to 37 years (The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: The lung disease generally determines CF patients' prognosis and causes ~90% of their morbidity and mortality.
source: Given that the lung disease generally determines CF patients' prognosis and causes ∼90% of their morbidity and mortality
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Staphylococcus aureus is a main cause of early infection in the lungs of CF patients.
source: Staphylococcus aureus is a main cause of early infection in the lungs of CF patients (The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Most S. aureus strains, including methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), secrete SMase C.
source: Most S. aureus strains, including methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), secrete the pathogenic factor sphingomyelinase (SMase) C
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: SMase C hydrolysis of sphingomyelin surrounding CFTR protein profoundly suppresses CFTR activity.
source: Our group has previously discovered that SMase C hydrolysis of sphingomyelin surrounding CFTR protein profoundly suppresses CFTR activity (Ramu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to previous work.

claim: Bacteria can further diminish critical residual CFTR activity in CF patients.
source: Thus, bacteria can further diminish critical residual CFTR activity in CF patients, worsening the negative impact of mutations.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the finding that SMase C suppresses CFTR activity.

claim: By inhibiting CFTR, SMase C-producing bacteria can create a temporary condition analogous to CFTR deficiency in non-CF patients with lung infection.
source: By inhibiting CFTR, SMase C-producing bacteria can also create a temporary condition, analogous to CFTR deficiency, in non-CF patients with lung infection.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the finding that SMase C suppresses CFTR activity.

claim: SMase C strongly inhibits the activity of Kv1.3 voltage-gated K+ (Kv) channels of lymphocytes.
source: Additionally, compounding this already very serious problem, SMase C strongly inhibits the activity of Kv1.3 voltage-gated K+ (Kv) channels of lymphocytes (Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to previous work.

claim: Inhibition of Kv1.3 channels is well known to cause immunosuppression.
source: Inhibition of these channels is well known to cause immunosuppression (Chandy et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Natural B. anthracis produces little SMase C due to a 'defective' regulatory gene.
source: Natural B. anthracis, against which the live STI-1 (Sanitary Technical Institute, USSR) vaccine provides effective protection, produces little SMase C due to a 'defective' regulatory gene.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information.

claim: B. anthracis engineered to express high levels of SMase C remains lethal.
source: However, once B. anthracis is engineered to express high levels of SMase C, the resulting mutant not only remains lethal but also evades the host immunity elicited by the live vaccine because additional pathogenic mechanisms are generated (Pomerantsev et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: B. anthracis engineered to express high levels of SMase C evades host immunity elicited by the live vaccine.
source: However, once B. anthracis is engineered to express high levels of SMase C, the resulting mutant not only remains lethal but also evades the host immunity elicited by the live vaccine because additional pathogenic mechanisms are generated (Pomerantsev et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: CFTR channels are often activated experimentally by boosting the concentration of intracellular cAMP with a combination of forskolin and IBMX.
source: Experimentally, the CFTR channels are often activated by boosting the concentration of intracellular cAMP with a combination of the adenylate cyclase activator forskolin and the phosphodiesterase inhibitor isobutylmethylxanthine (IBMX) (Csanady et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: SMase C from S. aureus markedly diminishes CFTR current in Xenopus oocytes in a time-dependent manner.
source: Following exposure to extracellular SMase C from S. aureus, the CFTR current was markedly diminished in a time-dependent manner (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: SMase C suppresses native CFTR current in Calu-3 cells.
source: As in oocytes, SMase C suppressed CFTR current in Calu-3 cells (Figure 1G–I), a result confirming that this SMase C effect on CFTR activity is not unique to the oocyte heterologous expression system.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: The SMase C effect on CFTR activity is not unique to the oocyte heterologous expression system.
source: As in oocytes, SMase C suppressed CFTR current in Calu-3 cells (Figure 1G–I), a result confirming that this SMase C effect on CFTR activity is not unique to the oocyte heterologous expression system.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the observation that SMase C suppresses CFTR in both oocytes and Calu-3 cells.

claim: All three recombinant S. aureus SMase C isoforms suppressed CFTR current albeit with differing specific activity.
source: All three recombinant isoforms suppressed CFTR current albeit with differing specific activity (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Two S. aureus SMase C isoforms lost activity over 96 hr, and one retained full activity.
source: Two isoforms lost activity over 96 hr, and one retained full activity
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental observations.

claim: All three S. aureus SMase C isoforms exhibited measurable activity for at least 48 hr.
source: all three isoforms exhibited measurable activity for at least 48 hr
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental observations.

claim: Secreted SMase C can remain active for a considerable time following death of the bacteria.
source: It follows that secreted SMase C can remain active for a considerable time following death of the bacteria.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observation that SMase C isoforms retain activity for at least 48 hours.

claim: An effective means to counteract SMase C action would be important in limiting the negative impact of bacterial infection on the host.
source: Thus, while antibiotics remain critical in combating the infection, an effective means to counteract SMase C action would be important in limiting the negative impact of the bacterial infection on the host.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the observation that SMase C remains active after bacterial death.

claim: At levels beyond that required to achieve maximal CFTR activation, PKA's catalytic subunit significantly lessens suppression of CFTR current by SMase C.
source: We previously found that at levels beyond that required to achieve maximal CFTR activation, PKA's catalytic subunit significantly lessens suppression of CFTR current by SMase C (Ramu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to previous work.

claim: SMase C modifying the head group chemistry of sphingomyelin molecules surrounding CFTR makes activation of CFTR more energetically difficult.
source: This observation suggests that SMase C modifying the head group chemistry of sphingomyelin molecules surrounding CFTR makes activation of CFTR more energetically difficult
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis to explain the observation that PKA lessens SMase C suppression.

claim: SMase C action can be markedly overcome by 'over-phosphorylating' the channel's R-domain until all four sites are phosphorylated.
source: this SMase C action can be markedly overcome by 'over-phosphorylating' the channel's R-domain until all four sites are phosphorylated
evidence: This is stated as part of the hypothesis to explain the PKA effect.

claim: In the presence of a supersaturating level of PKA's catalytic subunit, SMase C suppressed only 25% of the wild-type CFTR current.
source: As a control, we showed that in the presence of a supersaturating level of PKA's catalytic subunit, SMase C suppressed only 25% of the wild-type CFTR current (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Under the same experimental condition with supersaturating PKA, SMase C suppressed 40–65% of the single-mutant CFTR channels' currents.
source: In contrast and as predicted, under the same experimental condition, SMase C suppressed 40–65% of the mutants' currents.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: A β adrenergic receptor agonist should alleviate the SMase C-caused suppression of CFTR current by boosting intracellular cAMP.
source: A second corollary of our hypothesis is that a β adrenergic receptor agonist should alleviate the SMase C-caused suppression of CFTR current by boosting intracellular cAMP.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on the hypothesis about SMase C mechanism.

claim: β receptor agonists are routinely used as bronchodilators in patients suffering from pulmonary infectious and inflammatory diseases.
source: In fact, β receptor agonists are routinely used as bronchodilators in patients suffering from pulmonary infectious and inflammatory diseases.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge.

claim: Application of β receptor agonists would not be contraindicated in cases of infection by SMase C-positive bacteria and likely be beneficial.
source: Thus, application of β receptor agonists would not be contraindicated in cases of infection by SMase C-positive bacteria and likely be beneficial.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the hypothesis about β agonists alleviating SMase C suppression.

claim: A β receptor agonist unlikely causes overphosphorylation of the R domain.
source: However, given that a β receptor agonist unlikely causes overphosphorylation of the R domain, it may only modestly counteract the SMase C-dependent suppression of CFTR current.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about the mechanism of β agonist action.

claim: A β receptor agonist may only modestly counteract the SMase C-dependent suppression of CFTR current.
source: However, given that a β receptor agonist unlikely causes overphosphorylation of the R domain, it may only modestly counteract the SMase C-dependent suppression of CFTR current.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the mechanism of β agonist action.

claim: The authors screened a chemical library (Spectrum 2000) consisting of approved drugs and natural products, each at 10 µM concentration.
source: As such, we screened a chemical library (Spectrum 2000) consisting of approved drugs and natural products, each at 10 µM concentration.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental approach.

claim: The authors employed a fluorescence-based assay (Amplex Red) involving a series of coupled enzymatic reactions.
source: We employed a fluorescence-based assay (Amplex Red) involving a series of coupled enzymatic reactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental approach.

claim: Of 27 compounds tested at 10 µM, only tannic acid exhibited a clear SMase C-antagonizing effect.
source: We found that, of those 27 compounds at 10 µM, only tannic acid exhibited a clear SMase C-antagonizing effect (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Tannic acid was effective at antagonizing SMase C at concentrations down to 200 nM.
source: Tannic acid was just as effective at concentrations down to 200 nM (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Tannic acid antagonizes SMase C of B. anthracis.
source: Furthermore, we found that it also antagonized SMase C of B. anthracis (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Tannic acid is known to interact with many other proteins with apparent Kd or EC50 between 8 µM and 150 mM.
source: Tannic acid is known to interact with many other proteins with apparent Kd or EC50 between 8 µM and 150 mM (Gabbott, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: High concentrations of tannic acid (5–50 mM) are often used to fix cells in EM studies.
source: Consequently, high concentrations of tannic acid (5–50 mM) are often used to fix cells in EM studies (Hayat, 1981; Afzelius, 1992; Bozzola and Russell, 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: An EC50 range of 50–100 nM observed in this study is by far the lowest concentration range at which tannic acid is found to bind effectively to a protein and/or to produce a meaningful biological effect.
source: To our knowledge, a EC50 range of 50–100 nM observed in our study is by far the lowest concentration range at which tannic acid is found to bind effectively to a protein and/or to produce a meaningful biological effect (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison with literature and supported by data in Figure 3F.

claim: Tannic acid has been reported to bind to the choline group of phosphatidylcholine (PC).
source: Although tannic acid has been reported to bind to the choline group of phosphatidylcholine (PC)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as background information.

claim: Tannic acid does not appear to antagonize SMase C activity by binding to PC and thereby preventing SMase C from accessing sphingomyelin.
source: it does not appear to antagonize SMase C activity by binding to PC and thereby preventing SMase C from accessing sphingomyelin because tannic acid binds to PC only at much higher concentrations than what is required to antagonize SMase C activity (Kalina and Pease, 1977; Simon et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the concentration difference and supported by citations.

claim: The EC50 (~50 nM) of tannic acid for antagonizing the SMase C-catalyzed sphingomyelin hydrolysis in a biochemical reaction is comparable to its EC50 (~100 nM) for antagonizing SMase C suppression of CFTR activity in a biological membrane.
source: Furthermore, the EC50 (∼50 nM) of tannic acid for antagonizing the SMase C-catalyzed sphingomyelin hydrolysis in a biochemical reaction (involving no PC) is comparable to its EC50 (∼100 nM) for antagonizing SMase C suppression of CFTR activity in a biological membrane (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: SMase D specifically hydrolyzes sphingomyelin.
source: Like SMase C, SMase D specifically hydrolyzes sphingomyelin (bottom panel, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SMase D removes only the choline group rather than the entire phosphocholine head group from sphingomyelin.
source: However, unlike SMase C, SMase D removes only the choline group rather than the entire phosphocholine head group from sphingomyelin
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge.

claim: SMase D leaves ceramide-1-phosphate instead of ceramide behind in the membrane.
source: leaving ceramide-1-phosphate instead of ceramide behind in the membrane
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge.

claim: SMase D suppresses CFTR activity.
source: Our group previously showed that SMase D also suppresses CFTR activity (Ramu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to previous work.

claim: Tannic acid at 300 nM slightly slowed down SMase D suppression of CFTR activity.
source: Here, we show that tannic acid at 300 nM slightly slowed down SMase D suppression of CFTR activity (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Tannic acid at 200 nM essentially eliminated SMase C suppression of CFTR activity.
source: In contrast, as shown above, tannic acid at 200 nM essentially eliminated SMase C suppression of CFTR activity (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Tannic acid antagonizes SMase C and SMase D with differing potency.
source: Thus, tannic acid antagonizes SMase C and SMase D with differing potency (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In lymphocytes, Kv1.3 channels help maintain a sufficiently negative resting membrane potential to sustain an adequate driving force for Ca2+ entry.
source: In lymphocytes, Kv1.3 channels help maintain a sufficiently negative resting membrane potential to sustain an adequate driving force for Ca2+ entry which acts as a key signal to activate lymphocytes (DeCoursey et al., 1984; Matteson and Deutsch, 1984; Cahalan and Chandy, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: Ca2+ entry acts as a key signal to activate lymphocytes.
source: In lymphocytes, Kv1.3 channels help maintain a sufficiently negative resting membrane potential to sustain an adequate driving force for Ca2+ entry which acts as a key signal to activate lymphocytes (DeCoursey et al., 1984; Matteson and Deutsch, 1984; Cahalan and Chandy, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: Inhibition of Kv1.3 channels causes immunosuppression, a finding that has stimulated the development of inhibitors of Kv1.3 as effective immunosuppressants to treat autoimmune diseases.
source: Consequently, inhibition of Kv1.3 channels causes immunosuppression, a finding that has stimulated the development of inhibitors of Kv1.3 as effective immunosuppressants to treat autoimmune diseases (Chandy et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: SMase C, by removing the phosphoryl head group of sphingomyelin molecules around Kv1.3 channels, profoundly diminishes these channels' activity.
source: On this backdrop, we previously showed that SMase C, by removing the phosphoryl head group of sphingomyelin molecules around Kv1.3 channels, profoundly diminishes these channels' activity (Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to previous work.

claim: Removal of the negatively charged phosphoryl group makes it energetically more difficult for positively charged voltage sensors to transition to the activated state.
source: The underlying mechanism is that removal of the negatively charged phosphoryl group makes it energetically more difficult for positively charged voltage sensors to transition to the activated state.
evidence: This is stated as the mechanism explaining SMase C inhibition of Kv1.3 channels.

claim: Tannic acid can effectively counteract suppression of Kv1.3 activity by SMase C.
source: Here, we find that tannic acid can also effectively counteract suppression of Kv1.3 activity by SMase C (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Tannic acid is a readily available and inexpensive natural product.
source: It is a readily available and inexpensive natural product
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as general knowledge.

claim: Tannic acid is widely and abundantly used in the food industry.
source: widely and abundantly used in the food industry
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as general knowledge.

claim: The US Food and Drug Administration terms tannic acid Generally Recognized As Safe (GRAS).
source: The US Food and Drug Administration terms it Generally Recognized As Safe (GRAS) (FDA, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: The use of tannic acid to treat various diseases was reported as early as 1850.
source: The use of tannic acid to treat various diseases was reported as early as 1850 (Alison, 1850; Allegrini and Costantini, 2012)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: Tannic acid has been used in the treatment of human diarrhea.
source: for example in the treatment of human diarrhea
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an example of historical use.

claim: Recently reported clinical doses of tannic acid are 0.5–1 g.
source: Recently reported clinical doses are 0.5–1 g (Bian et al., 2009)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: Clinical doses of tannic acid give an estimated concentration in human body fluids of 8–16 µM.
source: giving an estimated concentration in human body fluids of 8–16 µM
evidence: This is stated as a calculation based on the clinical dose.

claim: Clinical doses of tannic acid result in concentrations 40–80 times higher than required to antagonize SMase C action.
source: or 40–80 times higher than required to antagonize SMase C action
evidence: This is stated as a calculation comparing clinical concentrations to the EC50 for SMase C antagonism.

claim: The authors suggest that tannic acid be considered to protect against B. anthracis mutants engineered to over-express SMase C.
source: We suggest that tannic acid be considered in attempts to protect against B. anthracis mutants engineered to over-express SMase C, in the unfortunate event of an outbreak
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: The authors suggest that tannic acid be considered to lessen the harm caused by natural SMase C-positive bacteria including MRSA, in both CF and non-CF patients.
source: or to lessen the harm caused by natural SMase C-positive bacteria including MRSA, in both CF and non-CF patients
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation based on the study findings.
